title: Electrical Docs
text:
This site covers electricity on paper, in data, and in the equipment that carries it. It starts with the equations and circuit theory, works through three-phase power systems, single line diagrams and control, then moves to filters and signal processing, forecasts grid load from real demand data, and asks whether a home battery pays for itself. It ends with the practical kit: the electrical toolbox, what a switchboard contains, and the motor families. The newer pages are runnable: each works an example in code and checks it with assertions.
For microcontrollers, builds and industrial automation see Hardware Tools. For the general forecasting toolkit these pages build on see Time Series ML.

A reference sheet across mechanics, electricity and magnetism, waves and optics, thermodynamics, relativity, quantum and nuclear physics


Electromagnetic Equations
Maxwell’s equations, the Lorentz force, the EM wave equation, field energy and the Poynting vector, Faraday’s and Lenz’s laws, and radiation pressure

Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws, AC and DC circuits, capacitance and inductance, power, machines, semiconductors, digital electronics, control systems and safety

Superposition, source transformation, Thevenin, Norton and maximum power transfer, each checked against a nodal solution of one two-source circuit, and why power systems never run at the matched point


Three-Phase Power Systems
Phasors, star and delta, three-phase power and the power triangle, sizing a power factor correction bank, why transmission runs at high voltage, and a swing-equation simulation of grid frequency after a generator trip


Utility Single Line Diagrams
Reading a utility SLD from transmission to customer: symbols, ratings and protection numbers, bus arrangements, normally open points, and a per-unit fault level calculation down the diagram


Control Systems
A DC motor from physics model to transfer function, poles and step response, P against PI against PID, Bode plots with gain and phase margins, and a discrete 1 kHz PID with anti-windup

Not Covered Yet

No power electronics. Nothing on rectifiers, buck and boost converters or inverters, which are what connect solar panels and batteries to the three-phase grid.
No circuit transients. RC, RL and RLC step responses, and the switching surges they cause, appear only indirectly through the motor model in Control Systems.
No test and measurement page. Oscilloscopes and logic analysers are named in the tools list but never explained.
No protection grading. The SLD page computes fault levels, but nothing covers fuse and breaker time-current curves or how upstream and downstream devices are coordinated.

title: Stepper Motors
text:
A stepper has multiple coil groups (phases) around the stator and a toothed/magnetized rotor. Energizing phases in a fixed sequence pulls the rotor from tooth to tooth, one discrete step at a time.

Common resolution: 200 steps/revolution = 1.8 degrees per step (also 0.9 deg = 400 steps).
No feedback needed: count the steps you send and you know the position (as long as you never lose one).
Very high holding torque at standstill; the rotor is magnetically latched.

title: Stepper Motors
text:
3. Step Modes and Microstepping
How the driver energizes the coils sets the smoothness and resolution:








Mode
Coil pattern
Effect




Full step (wave)
One phase on at a time.
Lowest torque.


Full step (2-phase)
Two phases on.
Full rated torque.


Half step
Alternate 1 and 2 phases.
2x resolution, smoother.


Microstepping
Sine/cosine current levels per phase.
Up to 256x resolution, very smooth.



Microstepping drives each coil with a graded current (approximating sine/cosine) so the rotor settles between full steps. It improves smoothness and reduces resonance/noise, but the incremental holding torque per microstep is small, so effective positioning accuracy does not scale 1:1 with microstep count.

title: Stepper Motors
section: 4. How Drivers Are Controlled: Step / Direction
text:
4. How Drivers Are Controlled: Step / Direction
The dominant interface is STEP + DIR: the microcontroller does not switch coils directly; it just pulses a wire.
MCU ---> STEP pin: each rising edge = advance one (micro)step
MCU ---> DIR pin : HIGH = clockwise, LOW = counter-clockwise
MCU ---> EN pin  : enable/disable the driver outputs
MS1/MS2/MS3 pins : set microstep resolution (full ... 1/16, 1/32...)
Speed = STEP pulse frequency. Distance = number of STEP pulses. A key setting is the driver’s current limit (via a Vref potentiometer or register), which must match the motor’s rated coil current to avoid overheating or lost torque.
STEP:  _|-|_|-|_|-|_|-|_|-|_   (5 pulses = 5 microsteps)
DIR:   ---------------------   (held HIGH = one direction)

title: Stepper Motors
Stepper Motors
text:
6. Practical Considerations

Lost steps: If load exceeds torque or acceleration is too aggressive, the motor skips steps and position is silently wrong. Ramp speed and size with margin.
Torque vs. speed: Holding torque is highest at standstill and falls as step rate rises; there is a top speed beyond which it stalls.
Heat: Steppers draw full current even when holding still. Lower the hold current if the driver supports it.
Resonance: Mid-speed resonance can cause missed steps; microstepping and damping help.
Closed-loop steppers: Adding an encoder (e.g. servo-stepper hybrids) recovers lost steps and gives servo-like reliability while keeping stepper simplicity.

title: Electric Motors
text:
Every motor relies on the same core principle: a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force (the Lorentz force, F = B I L). Arrange conductors on a rotating body (the rotor) inside a fixed magnetic field (the stator), and that force becomes torque.







Part
Role




Stator
Stationary part that produces (or hosts) the magnetic field.


Rotor
Rotating part that carries current or magnets and produces torque.


Windings
Coils of wire that carry current and generate magnetic fields.


Commutator / ESC
Switches current direction to keep torque flowing one way.


Bearings
Support the shaft and allow smooth rotation.


Air gap
Small clearance between rotor and stator; smaller = stronger coupling.



Key relationships:

Torque is proportional to current: T = Kt * I
Back-EMF (voltage generated by rotation) is proportional to speed: V_bemf = Ke * w
Mechanical power out: P = T * w (torque times angular velocity)

title: Electric Motors
text:
3. DC Motors

3.1. Brushed DC
A brushed DC motor uses carbon brushes and a commutator to mechanically switch current in the rotor windings, keeping the torque in one direction as the rotor spins.

Pros: Cheap, simple to drive (just apply DC voltage), easy speed control via voltage.
Cons: Brushes wear out, generate sparks and EMI, lower efficiency, limited lifespan.
Control: Vary voltage (PWM) for speed; reverse polarity for direction (H-bridge).



3.2. Brushless DC (BLDC)
A BLDC motor puts the permanent magnets on the rotor and the windings on the stator. An electronic speed controller (ESC) energizes the stator coils in sequence, replacing the mechanical commutator.

Pros: High efficiency, high power density, long life (no brushes), quiet.
Cons: Requires an ESC and rotor-position sensing (Hall sensors or sensorless back-EMF).
Control: Trapezoidal (six-step) or sinusoidal (FOC) commutation via the ESC.

text:
4. Stepper Motors
A stepper motor divides a full rotation into a fixed number of discrete steps (commonly 200 steps = 1.8 degrees each). By energizing coils in sequence, the rotor moves one precise step at a time, enabling accurate open-loop positioning without feedback.








Type
Description
Application




Permanent Magnet
Magnetized rotor, coarse steps, low cost.
Simple positioning.


Variable Reluctance
Toothed iron rotor, no magnet.
Legacy / specialty.


Hybrid
Combines PM + reluctance; fine steps, high torque.
3D printers, CNC, cameras.




Microstepping: Driving coils with intermediate current levels subdivides each step (e.g. 1/16, 1/256) for smoother, finer motion.
Trade-off: Excellent low-speed holding torque and precision, but torque drops at high speed and steps can be lost if overloaded (no feedback).
Drivers: A4988, DRV8825, TMC2209 (silent, sensorless load detection).

title: Electric Motors
text:
5. AC Motors

5.1. Induction (Asynchronous)
The stator’s rotating magnetic field induces current in the rotor (no direct electrical connection). The rotor always spins slightly slower than the field, a difference called slip.

Squirrel-cage: Rugged, cheap, self-starting; the workhorse of industry.
Wound-rotor: External rotor resistance for high starting torque and speed control.
Control: A Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) changes the supply frequency to vary speed.



5.2. Synchronous
The rotor locks to and rotates exactly at the supply frequency (no slip). Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors (PMSM) are the high-efficiency choice for EV traction and servo drives.

5.3. Universal
A series-wound motor that runs on either AC or DC. High speed and good starting torque make it ideal for handheld power tools and vacuum cleaners, at the cost of brush wear and noise.

Key control concepts:

PWM (Pulse Width Modulation): Rapidly switch power on/off; the average voltage sets speed.
H-Bridge: Four switches that let current flow through a motor in either direction, enabling forward/reverse and braking.
FOC (Field-Oriented Control): Controls the motor’s current vector for smooth, efficient torque; the standard for high-performance BLDC/PMSM drives.
Closed vs. open loop: Servos use encoder feedback (closed loop) for accuracy; steppers usually run open loop.

title: Electric Motors
text:
7. Key Specifications
When selecting a motor, these are the numbers that matter:







Spec
Meaning




Voltage (V)
Nominal operating voltage.


Current / Stall Current
Running current and worst-case locked-rotor current.


Torque (N.m or kg.cm)
Rotational force; rated vs. stall (max) torque.


Speed (RPM)
No-load speed; drops under load.


Kv (for BLDC)
RPM per volt with no load (higher Kv = faster, lower torque).


Power (W)
Mechanical output = torque x angular velocity.


Efficiency (%)
Mechanical power out / electrical power in.


Duty cycle
Continuous vs. intermittent operation rating.



A motor’s torque-speed curve captures most of this: torque is highest at stall (zero speed) and falls linearly to zero at no-load speed; peak power sits near the middle.

Rules of thumb:

Match stall torque with margin above your worst-case load; do not size to rated torque alone.
Check the stall current your driver and power supply must survive.
For battery devices, prioritize efficiency (BLDC/PMSM) to extend runtime.
For anything that must hold or step to exact positions cheaply, use a stepper; if it must not lose position under load, use a servo.

title: Nixtla - Detect Demand Peaks
text:
Predicting peaks in different markets is useful. In the electricity market, consuming electricity at peak demand is penalized with higher tarifs. When an individual or company consumes electricity when its most demanded, regulators calls that a coincident peak (CP).
In the Texas electricity market (ERCOT), the peak is the monthly 15-minute interval when the ERCOT Grid is at a point of highest capacity. The peak is caused by all consumers’ combined demand on the electrical grid. The coincident peak demand is an important factor used by ERCOT to determine final electricity consumption bills. ERCOT registers the CP demand of each client for 4 months, between June and September, and uses this to adjust electricity prices. Clients can therefore save on electricity bills by reducing the coincident peak demand.
In this example we will train an MSTL (Multiple Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS) model on historic load data to forecast day-ahead peaks on September 2022. Multiple seasonality is traditionally present in low sampled electricity data. Demand exhibits daily and weekly seasonality, with clear patterns for specific hours of the day such as 6:00pm vs 3:00am or for specific days such as Sunday vs Friday.
First, we will load ERCOT historic demand, then we will use the StatsForecast.cross_validation method to fit the MSTL model and forecast daily load during September. Finally, we show how to use the forecasts to detect the coincident peak.

text:
Fit and Forecast MSTL model
The MSTL (Multiple Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS) model decomposes the time series in multiple seasonalities using a Local Polynomial Regression (LOESS). Then it forecasts the trend using a custom non-seasonal model and each seasonality using a SeasonalNaive model.






Tip



Check our detailed explanation and tutorial on MSTL here


Import the StatsForecast class and the models you need.

from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import MSTL, AutoARIMA

First, instantiate the model and define the parameters. The electricity load presents seasonalities every 24 hours (Hourly) and every 24 * 7 (Daily) hours. Therefore, we will use [24, 24 * 7] as the seasonalities. See this link for a detailed explanation on how to set seasonal lengths. In this example we use the AutoARIMA model for the trend component, however, any StatsForecast model can be used. The complete list of models is available here.

models = [MSTL(
            season_length=[24, 24 * 7], # seasonalities of the time series 
            trend_forecaster=AutoARIMA(nmodels=10) # model used to forecast trend
            )
          ]







Tip



The parameter nmodels of the AutoARIMA controls the number of models considered in stepwise search. The default is 94, reduce it to decrease training times!


We fit the model by instantiating a StatsForecast object with the following required parameters:

models: a list of models. Select the models you want from models and import them.
freq: a string indicating the frequency of the data. (See panda’s available frequencies.)


# Instantiate StatsForecast class as sf
sf = StatsForecast(
    df=Y_df, 
    models=models,
    freq='H', 
)







Tip



StatsForecast also supports this optional parameter.

n_jobs: n_jobs: int, number of jobs used in the parallel processing, use -1 for all cores. (Default: 1)
fallback_model: a model to be used if a model fails. (Default: none)



The cross_validation method allows the user to simulate multiple historic forecasts, greatly simplifying pipelines by replacing for loops with fit and predict methods. This method re-trains the model and forecast each window. See this tutorial for an animation of how the windows are defined.
Use the cross_validation method to produce all the daily forecasts for September. To produce daily forecasts set the forecasting horizon h as 24. In this example we are simulating deploying the pipeline during September, so set the number of windows as 30 (one for each day). Finally, set the step size between windows as 24, to only produce one forecast per day.

crossvalidation_df = sf.cross_validation(
    df=Y_df,
    h=24,
    step_size=24,
    n_windows=30
  )

title: Nixtla - Detect Demand Peaks
text:
Peak Detection
Finally, we use the forecasts in crossvaldation_df to detect the daily hourly demand peaks. For each day, we set the detected peaks as the highest forecasts. In this case, we want to predict one peak (npeaks); depending on your setting and goals, this parameter might change. For example, the number of peaks can correspond to how many hours a battery can be discharged to reduce demand.

npeaks = 1 # Number of peaks

For the ERCOT 4CP detection task we are interested in correctly predicting the highest monthly load. Next, we filter the day in September with the highest hourly demand and predict the peak.

crossvalidation_df = crossvalidation_df.reset_index()[['ds','y','MSTL']]
max_day = crossvalidation_df.iloc[crossvalidation_df['y'].argmax()].ds.day # Day with maximum load
cv_df_day = crossvalidation_df.query('ds.dt.day == @max_day')
max_hour = cv_df_day['y'].argmax()
peaks = cv_df_day['MSTL'].argsort().iloc[-npeaks:].values # Predicted peaks

In the following plot we see how the MSTL model is able to correctly detect the coincident peak for September 2022.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.axvline(cv_df_day.iloc[max_hour]['ds'], color='black', label='True Peak')
plt.scatter(cv_df_day.iloc[peaks]['ds'], cv_df_day.iloc[peaks]['MSTL'], color='green', label=f'Predicted Top-{npeaks}')
plt.plot(cv_df_day['ds'], cv_df_day['y'], label='y', color='blue')
plt.plot(cv_df_day['ds'], cv_df_day['MSTL'], label='Forecast', color='red')
plt.xlabel('Time')
plt.ylabel('Load (MW)')
plt.grid()
plt.legend()














Important



In this example we only include September. However, MSTL can correctly predict the peaks for the 4 months of 2022. You can try this by increasing the nwindows parameter of cross_validation or filtering the Y_df dataset. The complete run for all months take only 10 minutes.

The plot below shows us that a simple DFT with a random train-test split will most likely lead to bad results. Upon closer inspection we can see that the prediction (in purple) simply repeats the training set (blue). This is the standard behavior of the DFT, and by itself it is quite useless, since repeating our training set could be done much more efficiently. Three improvements were made to this approach.

title: Darts - Fast Fourier Transform Forecasting Model (FFT)
text:
Improvement 1: Crop the training set
The first improvement consists of cropping the training set before feeding it to the FFT algorithm such that the first timestamp in the cropped series matches the first timestamp to be predicted in terms of seasonality, i.e. it has the same month, day, weekday, time of day, etc. We could achieve this by passing the optional argument required_matches to the FFT constructor that explicitly tells our model which timestamp attributes are relevant. But actually, if we don’t set it manually, the model will attempt to automatically find the pd.Timestamp attributes that are relevant and crop the training set accordingly (which we will do here).


model = FFT(nr_freqs_to_keep=None)
model.fit(train)
pred_val = model.predict(len(val))

We can see that the results look like the seasonality of the predictions nicely aligns with the seasonality of the validation set. However, we are still just repeating the training set, including all of the noise. Looking at the error we can see that this is still a pretty bad forecast.

train.plot(label="train")
val.plot(label="val")
pred_val.plot(label="predict")
print("MAE:", mae(pred_val, val))

title: Darts - Fast Fourier Transform Forecasting Model (FFT)
text:
Improvement 2: Filtering out low-amplitude waves
The decomposition of the DFT into the frequency domain allows us to selectively filter out waves with low amplitudes. This allows us to keep strong seasonal trends while discarding some noise. This is achieved in the FFT model by passing the optional argument nr_freqs_to_keep. This argument represents the total number of frequencies that will be kept. For instance, if a value of 20 is passed, only the 20 frequencies with the highest amplitudes will be utilized. The default value is set to 10.


model = FFT(nr_freqs_to_keep=20)
model.fit(train)
pred_val = model.predict(len(val))

We get a signal that is less noisy. Depending on the data set, this might be a better forecast. Looking at the error metric, we can see that this model performs significantly better than the previous models.

val.plot(label="val")
pred_val.plot(label="predict")

model.fit(train)
pred_val = model.predict(len(val))

We have a much better prediction now.

title: Control Systems
text:
A control system makes a physical thing follow a command: a motor holds its speed, an oven holds its temperature, a drone holds its height. This page takes one plant, a small DC motor, from a physics model to a tuned PID (proportional, integral, derivative) controller running in discrete time. The tools along the way are transfer functions, poles, step responses and Bode plots.
The analysis uses scipy.signal. Every design claim is checked by assertions against a simulation.

title: Control Systems
text:
Why feedback



Feedback loop: the set point r and the measured speed y meet at a summing junction to form the error e; the PID controller C(s) turns the error into a voltage u; the plant G(s), a DC motor, turns voltage into speed y, which is measured and fed back.


An open-loop controller computes the voltage once, from a model, and hopes. It fails as soon as the model is wrong or something pushes on the motor: a heavier load, a cold bearing, a sagging supply. A closed-loop controller measures the output, compares it with the set point, and acts on the error. Feedback buys two things: it rejects disturbances, and it makes the result insensitive to errors in the model.
The price is that feedback can make a stable plant unstable. A controller that reacts too hard, or too late, overshoots, over-corrects, and oscillates. Most of control engineering is about getting the benefit without paying that price.

title: Control Systems
text:
Transfer functions
The motor has a mechanical side and an electrical side. Torque is proportional to current, \(\tau = K i\). The spinning armature generates a back-EMF (electromotive force) proportional to speed, \(e = K\omega\):
\[J\dot\omega + b\,\omega = K i \qquad L\,\dot i + R\,i = V - K\omega\]
Here \(J\) is rotor inertia, \(b\) viscous friction, \(L\) and \(R\) the winding inductance and resistance, and \(K\) the motor constant. The Laplace transform turns each derivative into a multiplication by \(s\), so the differential equations become algebra. Eliminating \(i\) gives the transfer function from voltage to speed:
\[G(s) = \frac{\Omega(s)}{V(s)} = \frac{K}{(Js + b)(Ls + R) + K^2}\]
A transfer function is the whole input-output behaviour of a linear system in one ratio of polynomials. The roots of the denominator, the poles, set how the system moves on its own.

import numpy as np
from pyecharts import options as opts
from pyecharts.charts import Line, Bar
from pyecharts.globals import CurrentConfig

J, b, K, R, L = 0.01, 0.1, 0.01, 1.0, 0.5    # kg m^2, N m s, N m/A, ohm, H
num = np.array([K])
den = np.polyadd(np.polymul([J, b], [L, R]), [K**2])
G = signal.TransferFunction(num, den)
poles = np.roots(den)
dc_gain = num[0] / den[-1]
print("G(s) =", np.round(num, 4), "/", np.round(den, 4))
print("poles:", np.round(poles, 4), "  DC gain:", round(dc_gain, 4), "(rad/s) per V")

t = np.linspace(0, 4, 201)
_, y_open = signal.step(G, T=t)
step_chart = (
    Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="320px"))

    .add_yaxis("speed for a 1 V step", [round(float(v), 5) for v in y_open], is_symbol_show=False)
    .set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=False))
    .set_global_opts(
        title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="Open loop: motor speed after a 1 V step"),
        xaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="s", boundary_gap=False),
        yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="rad/s"),

G(s) = [0.01] / [0.005  0.06   0.1001]
poles: [-9.9975 -2.0025]   DC gain: 0.0999 (rad/s) per V





        




The poles sit at about \(-2\) and \(-10\) per second. Both are real and negative, so the motor is stable and does not oscillate on its own. The pole at \(-2\) is slow, with a time constant of 0.5 s. It is the mechanical lag of spinning up the rotor, and it dominates the response. The pole at \(-10\) is the electrical lag of the winding. One volt gives only 0.1 rad/s and takes about 2 s to get there. A controller must do much better than that.

title: Control Systems
text:
Poles and stability
Each pole \(p\) contributes a term \(e^{pt}\) to the response. That one fact gives the whole stability picture:








Pole location
Term \(e^{pt}\)
Behaviour




Negative real
Decaying exponential
Stable, no overshoot


Complex pair, negative real part
Decaying oscillation
Stable, overshoot and ringing


On the imaginary axis
Constant oscillation
On the edge of stability


Positive real part
Growing
Unstable



A second-order system with poles \(s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = 0\) is described by its natural frequency \(\omega_n\), which sets the speed, and its damping ratio \(\zeta\), which sets the overshoot. At \(\zeta = 1\) it is critically damped. Below 1 it overshoots, by about 5 % at \(\zeta = 0.7\) and 16 % at \(\zeta = 0.5\).
Feedback moves the poles. With controller \(C(s)\), the loop transfer function is \(L(s) = C(s)G(s)\), and the closed loop from set point to output is:
\[T(s) = \frac{L(s)}{1 + L(s)}\]
The closed-loop poles are the roots of \(1 + L(s) = 0\). Designing a controller means choosing \(C(s)\) to put those roots where you want them.

title: Control Systems
text:
PID control
A PID controller adds three reactions to the error \(e(t)\):
\[u(t) = K_p\,e(t) + K_i\int_0^t e\,d\tau + K_d\,\frac{de}{dt} \qquad C(s) = K_p + \frac{K_i}{s} + K_d\,s\]

P pushes in proportion to the error now. On its own, it always leaves a steady-state error, because it needs a nonzero error to produce any output at all.
I pushes in proportion to the error accumulated so far. It keeps growing until the error is exactly zero, which removes the steady-state error. Too much makes the loop oscillate.
D pushes against the rate of change of the error. It anticipates, adding damping. It also amplifies measurement noise, so real controllers filter it.

The cell compares three designs on the motor:

P only, \(K_p = 100\).
PI with its zero placed on the slow pole: \(K_i/K_p = 2\). The integrator’s zero cancels the motor’s mechanical lag. That leaves \(L(s) = 60/(s(s+10))\), a well-damped second-order loop.
PID with both zeros placed on both poles: \(C(s) = K_d (s - p_1)(s - p_2)/s\). Then \(L(s) = K_d K/(JL)\,/\,s = 2K_d/s\), a pure integrator, and the closed loop is first order with time constant \(1/(2K_d)\). With \(K_d = 5\) that is 0.1 s.


def closed_loop(c_num, c_den):
    "Closed loop T = CG / (1 + CG) as a TransferFunction."
    l_num, l_den = np.polymul(c_num, num), np.polymul(c_den, den)
    return signal.TransferFunction(l_num, np.polyadd(l_den, l_num))

a1, a0 = den[1] / den[0], den[2] / den[0]    # den / J L = s^2 + a1 s + a0
Kd = 5.0
designs = {
    "P   (Kp=100)":            ([100.0], [1.0]),
    "PI  (Kp=30, Ki=60)":      ([30.0, 60.0], [1.0, 0.0]),
    f"PID (Kp={Kd * a1:.0f}, Ki={Kd * a0:.0f}, Kd={Kd:.0f})": ([Kd, Kd * a1, Kd * a0], [1.0, 0.0]),
}
t = np.linspace(0, 1.5, 151)
results = {}
for name, (cn, cd) in designs.items():
    T = closed_loop(cn, cd)
    _, y = signal.step(T, T=t)
    final = T.num[-1] / T.den[-1]
    overshoot = max(0.0, 100 * (y.max() - final) / final)
    t_settle = t[np.where(np.abs(y - final) > 0.02 * final)[0][-1] + 1]
    results[name] = dict(y=y, poles=np.roots(T.den), final=final)
    print(f"{name:26s} final {final:.3f}  steady-state error {100 * (1 - final):5.1f} %  "
          f"overshoot {overshoot:4.1f} %  2 % settling {t_settle:.2f} s")

cmp_chart = Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="340px")).add_xaxis([f"{x:.2f}" for x in t])
for name, r in results.items():
    cmp_chart.add_yaxis(name.split("(")[0].strip(), [round(float(v), 4) for v in r["y"]], is_symbol_show=False)
cmp_chart = cmp_chart.set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=False)).set_global_opts(
    title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="Closed loop: speed after a 1 rad/s set-point step"),
    xaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="s", boundary_gap=False),
    yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="rad/s"),
    tooltip_opts=opts.TooltipOpts(trigger="axis"),
    legend_opts=opts.LegendOpts(pos_top="8%"),
)
cmp_chart.render_notebook()

P   (Kp=100)               final 0.909  steady-state error   9.1 %  overshoot 24.9 %  2 % settling 0.57 s
PI  (Kp=30, Ki=60)         final 1.000  steady-state error   0.0 %  overshoot  7.0 %  2 % settling 0.78 s
PID (Kp=60, Ki=100, Kd=5)  final 1.000  steady-state error   0.0 %  overshoot  0.0 %  2 % settling 0.40 s





        




P alone settles 9 % short of the set point and rings on the way. Raising \(K_p\) shrinks the error but makes the ringing worse. PI removes the error, with a modest overshoot. The cancellation PID gives a clean first-order rise with a 0.1 s time constant, exactly as designed.
Cancellation is a teaching design, not a robust one. It relies on knowing the poles exactly. If the motor’s real inertia is 20 % higher, the cancellation is imperfect, and a slow tail appears in the response. In practice, engineers tune against margins, which the next section covers. When no model exists at all, the classic Ziegler-Nichols experiment finds one by test: raise \(K_p\) alone until the loop oscillates steadily at gain \(K_u\) with period \(T_u\), then set \(K_p = 0.6K_u\), \(T_i = T_u/2\) and \(T_d = T_u/8\). The result is aggressive, and it is usually a starting point for hand tuning.

title: Control Systems
text:
Bode plots and stability margins
A Bode plot shows how a system responds to sine waves of each frequency: gain in decibels (\(20\log_{10}|L|\)) and phase shift, both against log frequency. Applied to the loop \(L(s) = C(s)G(s)\), it shows how close the closed loop is to instability, without solving for any poles.
The loop goes unstable if a signal can travel round it and come back the same size and inverted, which is a gain of 1 (0 dB) with a phase of \(-180\) degrees. The two margins measure the distance from that point:

Phase margin: at the frequency where \(|L| = 1\) (the crossover frequency), how far the phase is above \(-180\) degrees. Aim for 45 to 60 degrees or more.
Gain margin: at the frequency where the phase reaches \(-180\) degrees, how far the gain is below 0 dB. Aim for 6 dB or more.

A real derivative term is always filtered. Here \(K_d s\) becomes \(K_d s / (T_f s + 1)\) with \(T_f = 0.01\) s. The filter costs a little phase near crossover, and the margins below include that cost.

Kp, Ki, Tf = Kd * a1, Kd * a0, 0.01
c_num = np.polyadd(np.polymul([Kp, Ki], [Tf, 1.0]), [Kd, 0.0, 0.0])   # (Kp s + Ki)(Tf s + 1) + Kd s^2
c_den = np.polymul([1.0, 0.0], [Tf, 1.0])                            # s (Tf s + 1)
Lsys = signal.TransferFunction(np.polymul(c_num, num), np.polymul(c_den, den))

w = np.logspace(-1, 3, 161)
_, mag, phase = signal.bode(Lsys, w)
_, mag_g, _ = signal.bode(G, w)
i_c = np.argmin(np.abs(mag))
w_c, pm = w[i_c], 180 + phase[i_c]
gm = "infinite (phase never reaches -180 deg)" if phase.min() > -180 else f"{-np.interp(-180, phase[::-1], mag[::-1]):.1f} dB"
print(f"crossover {w_c:.2f} rad/s, phase margin {pm:.1f} deg, gain margin {gm}")

bode = (
    Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="360px"))
    .add_xaxis([f"{x:.3g}" for x in w])
    .add_yaxis("|L| loop gain (dB)", [round(float(v), 2) for v in mag], is_symbol_show=False)
    .add_yaxis("|G| motor alone (dB)", [round(float(v), 2) for v in mag_g], is_symbol_show=False)
    .add_yaxis("loop phase (deg)", [round(float(v), 2) for v in phase], is_symbol_show=False, yaxis_index=1,
               linestyle_opts=opts.LineStyleOpts(type_="dashed"))
    .extend_axis(yaxis=opts.AxisOpts(name="phase (deg)", min_=-180, max_=0, interval=45))
    .set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=False))
    .set_global_opts(
        title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="Bode plot of the PID loop"),
        xaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="rad/s (log)", boundary_gap=False),
        yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="gain (dB)"),
        tooltip_opts=opts.TooltipOpts(trigger="axis"),
        legend_opts=opts.LegendOpts(pos_top="8%"),
    )
)
bode.render_notebook()

crossover 10.59 rad/s, phase margin 87.3 deg, gain margin infinite (phase never reaches -180 deg)





        




The loop gain falls at a steady 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB near 10 rad/s, the bandwidth the design asked for. The phase sits near \(-90\) degrees and only starts to sag at high frequency, where the derivative filter acts. A phase margin above 80 degrees and an infinite gain margin make this a very safe loop. The price is speed: the design asked for a 0.1 s time constant and nothing faster. Comparing \(|L|\) with \(|G|\) shows what the controller did. It added gain at low frequency, where the motor was too weak, and none at high frequency, where noise lives.

title: Control Systems
text:
Discrete PID with anti-windup
Real controllers run on a microcontroller, sampling the speed every \(\Delta t\) and updating the voltage once per sample. The continuous design carries over directly if \(\Delta t\) is much faster than the loop. Here the loop runs at 1 kHz against a 10 rad/s bandwidth. The integral becomes a running sum, and the filtered derivative becomes a one-line recursive update.
Real actuators also have limits. This motor driver cannot apply more than 12 V. While the output is pinned at the limit, the error stays large, and the integral keeps growing. That stored-up integral then has to be unwound by overshooting the other way. This is integrator windup. The simplest fix is conditional integration: stop integrating while the output is saturated and the error would push it further into saturation.
The cell runs three cases with a 1 rad/s step, which needs 10 V in steady state:

No limit, to confirm the discrete loop matches the continuous design.
A 12 V limit, with a naive integrator.
A 12 V limit, with conditional integration.


dt, t_end = 1e-3, 6.0
Ad, Bd, Cd, Dd, _ = signal.cont2discrete(signal.tf2ss(num, den), dt, method="zoh")

def run_pid(u_max=np.inf, anti_windup=False, r=1.0):
    "Discrete PID (filtered derivative) driving the ZOH-discretised motor."
    x = np.zeros((Ad.shape[0], 1))
    integ = d = e_prev = 0.0
    ys, us = [], []
    for _ in range(int(round(t_end / dt))):
        y = float((Cd @ x)[0, 0])
        e = r - y
        d = (Tf * d + Kd * (e - e_prev)) / (Tf + dt)      # backward-Euler filtered derivative
        u_raw = Kp * e + integ + d
        u = float(np.clip(u_raw, -u_max, u_max))
        saturated = u != u_raw
        if not (anti_windup and saturated and np.sign(e) == np.sign(u_raw)):
            integ += Ki * e * dt
        x = Ad @ x + Bd * u
        e_prev = e
        ys.append(y); us.append(u)
    return np.array(ys), np.array(us)

tk = np.arange(int(round(t_end / dt))) * dt
y_free, _ = run_pid()
y_wind, u_wind = run_pid(u_max=12.0)
y_aw, u_aw = run_pid(u_max=12.0, anti_windup=True)

T_cont = signal.TransferFunction(np.polymul(c_num, num), np.polyadd(np.polymul(c_den, den), np.polymul(c_num, num)))
_, y_cont = signal.step(T_cont, T=tk)
print(f"no limit: discrete vs continuous, worst difference {np.abs(y_free - y_cont).max():.4f} rad/s")
for name, y in [("12 V limit, naive integrator", y_wind), ("12 V limit, anti-windup", y_aw)]:
    print(f"{name:30s} peak {y.max():.3f} rad/s, overshoot {max(0.0, 100 * (y.max() - 1)):5.1f} %")

idx = np.arange(0, len(tk), 30)
sat_chart = (
    Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="340px"))
    .add_xaxis([f"{x:.3f}" for x in tk[idx]])
    .add_yaxis("no limit", [round(float(v), 4) for v in y_free[idx]], is_symbol_show=False)
    .add_yaxis("12 V, naive integrator", [round(float(v), 4) for v in y_wind[idx]], is_symbol_show=False)
    .add_yaxis("12 V, anti-windup", [round(float(v), 4) for v in y_aw[idx]], is_symbol_show=False)
    .set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=False))
    .set_global_opts(
        title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="Discrete PID at 1 kHz, with and without a 12 V limit"),
        xaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="s", boundary_gap=False),
        yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="rad/s"),
        tooltip_opts=opts.TooltipOpts(trigger="axis"),
        legend_opts=opts.LegendOpts(pos_top="8%"),
    )
)
sat_chart.render_notebook()

no limit: discrete vs continuous, worst difference 0.0032 rad/s
12 V limit, naive integrator   peak 1.187 rad/s, overshoot  18.7 %
12 V limit, anti-windup        peak 1.000 rad/s, overshoot   0.0 %





        




Without a limit, the 1 kHz loop tracks the continuous design to within a fraction of a percent. With the 12 V limit, the motor can only accelerate so fast, so both limited runs rise slowly. The naive integrator charges up during that long climb, then drives the speed almost 19 % past the set point and takes seconds to unwind. Conditional integration stops the charging, so the speed never overshoots. It pays for that with a slower final approach from below, because the integral only starts building once the output leaves the limit. A refinement called back-calculation bleeds the integral towards the value the limit allows, instead of freezing it, and recovers some of that time. Every serious PID implementation, from a drone flight controller to an industrial drive, includes some form of anti-windup for this reason.

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
text:
Almost all electricity is generated, transmitted and used as three-phase alternating current. In Australia, a house gets one phase at 230 V. A workshop or a factory gets all three at 400 V between lines. The grid runs at 50 Hz (60 Hz in the Americas). This page builds up the tools in order: phasors, then three phases, then power and power factor, then transmission, and last, how a grid keeps supply equal to demand every second.
Each section computes a worked example and checks it with assertions. The numbers use the Australian low-voltage standard of 230/400 V, 50 Hz.

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
text:
Phasors
A steady sine wave \(v(t) = V_m \cos(\omega t + \phi)\) is fully described by two numbers: its size and its phase angle. Frequency is the same everywhere in the circuit, so it can be left out. A phasor packs the two numbers into one complex number, \(V = V_{rms}\angle\phi\). Engineers use the RMS (root mean square) value, \(V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt{2}\), because it gives the same heating as DC of that size. “230 V” means 230 V RMS, which peaks at 325 V.
Inductors and capacitors then become complex impedances: \(Z_L = j\omega L\) and \(Z_C = 1/(j\omega C)\). With \(Z = R + jX\), Ohm’s law works unchanged, \(I = V/Z\). Python’s built-in complex type does the arithmetic. Python writes \(j\) as 1j.

import numpy as np
from pyecharts import options as opts
from pyecharts.charts import Line, Bar
from pyecharts.globals import CurrentConfig

# assets.pyecharts.org served an expired TLS cert on 2026-11-11; pin the jsDelivr mirror
CurrentConfig.ONLINE_HOST = "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/pyecharts/pyecharts-assets@f2328d558550046fc5449672a6850e848e141590/assets/v6/"
import cmath
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

f0 = 50.0                 # Hz
w = 2 * np.pi * f0        # rad/s
V_ph = 230.0              # V rms, line to neutral

def polar(z, unit=""):
    "Format a complex number as magnitude and angle in degrees."
    return f"{abs(z):.2f}{unit} at {np.degrees(cmath.phase(z)):+.2f} deg"

Z = 8 + 6j                # ohm: 8 ohm resistance, 6 ohm inductive reactance
L = 6 / w                 # the inductance that gives X = 6 ohm at 50 Hz
I = V_ph / Z
pf = np.cos(cmath.phase(Z))
print(f"Z = {polar(Z, ' ohm')}   (L = {L * 1e3:.2f} mH)")
print(f"I = {polar(I, ' A')}")
print(f"power factor = {pf:.2f} lagging; P = {V_ph * abs(I) * pf:.0f} W")

Z = 10.00 ohm at +36.87 deg   (L = 19.10 mH)
I = 23.00 A at -36.87 deg
power factor = 0.80 lagging; P = 4232 W


The current is 23 A and lags the voltage by 36.9 degrees, because the inductor resists changes in current. The cosine of that angle, 0.8, is the power factor. Only the part of the current in phase with the voltage delivers energy.

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
text:
Three phases
A three-phase generator has three windings spaced 120 degrees apart around its rotor, so it produces three sine waves 120 degrees apart in time. Two properties make this the standard everywhere.

The three currents sum to zero when the loads are balanced, so a single neutral wire carries almost nothing. Three circuits need three or four wires instead of six.
Total power is constant, not pulsing. A single-phase load draws power in pulses at twice the line frequency. Three phases add up to a flat line. That is why three-phase motors run smoothly and are self-starting.


t = np.linspace(0, 0.04, 161)             # two cycles at 50 Hz, 0.25 ms steps
Vm = np.sqrt(2) * V_ph
phi = cmath.phase(Z)
shifts = [0, -2 * np.pi / 3, 2 * np.pi / 3]
v = [Vm * np.cos(w * t + s) for s in shifts]
i = [Vm / abs(Z) * np.cos(w * t + s - phi) for s in shifts]
p = [vk * ik for vk, ik in zip(v, i)]
v_sum, p_total = sum(v), sum(p)

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
text:
Star and delta
There are two ways to connect three loads, or three windings, to three lines.



Star connection: three impedances Z meet at a neutral point N, with lines L1, L2 and L3 at their outer ends; phase voltage 230 V, line voltage 400 V, line current equals phase current. Delta connection: three impedances form a triangle between the lines; phase voltage equals line voltage of 400 V, line current is root 3 times phase current, and there is no neutral.



Star (wye, Y). Each load sits between a line and the neutral, so it sees the phase voltage, 230 V. The voltage between two lines is the difference of two phasors 120 degrees apart. That difference is \(\sqrt{3}\) times larger and leads by 30 degrees: \(V_L = \sqrt{3}\,V_{ph} = 400\) V.
Delta (\(\Delta\)). Each load sits between two lines, so it sees the full line voltage, 400 V. Each line current is now the difference of two load currents: \(I_L = \sqrt{3}\,I_{ph}\).

The cell below checks the \(\sqrt{3}\) and the 30 degrees with phasor arithmetic. It also checks the star-delta equivalence for balanced loads: a delta of \(Z\) draws the same line current as a star of \(Z/3\).

a = cmath.rect(1, 2 * np.pi / 3)          # the 120 degree rotation operator
Va, Vb, Vc = V_ph, V_ph * a**2, V_ph * a   # positive sequence: A, then B 120 deg later
Vab = Va - Vb
print(f"Va  = {polar(Va, ' V')}")
print(f"Vab = {polar(Vab, ' V')}   ratio |Vab|/|Va| = {abs(Vab) / abs(Va):.4f} = sqrt(3)")

Zd = 3 * Z                                 # a delta of 3Z ...
I_ab, I_ca = Vab / Zd, (Vc - Va) / Zd
I_line_delta = I_ab - I_ca
I_line_star = Va / Z                       # ... matches a star of Z
print(f"delta of 3Z: line current {polar(I_line_delta, ' A')}")
print(f"star of Z:   line current {polar(I_line_star, ' A')}")

Va  = 230.00 V at +0.00 deg
Vab = 398.37 V at +30.00 deg   ratio |Vab|/|Va| = 1.7321 = sqrt(3)
delta of 3Z: line current 23.00 A at -36.87 deg
star of Z:   line current 23.00 A at -36.87 deg


The same factor is behind star-delta starting of large motors. Started in star, each winding sees \(1/\sqrt{3}\) of its rated voltage, so it draws one third of the current and makes one third of the torque. Once the motor is up to speed, a contactor switches the windings to delta.

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
section: Three-phase power and the power triangle
text:
Three-phase power and the power triangle
For a balanced load, the power in each phase is the same, so the total is three times one phase. Written with line quantities, which are what you can measure on the cables:
\[P = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \cos\phi \qquad Q = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \sin\phi \qquad S = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L\]

\(P\) is real power, in watts. It does work and turns the meter.
\(Q\) is reactive power, in volt-amperes reactive (var). It is energy that sloshes back and forth into magnetic fields each cycle. It does no net work, but it still flows in the cables.
\(S\) is apparent power, in volt-amperes (VA). It sets the current, and therefore the size of every cable, fuse and transformer.

The three form a right triangle, \(S^2 = P^2 + Q^2\), and the power factor is \(P/S\). As a complex number, \(S = P + jQ = 3\,V_{ph} I_{ph}^*\), where \(^*\) is the complex conjugate.
The example is a workshop motor load of 30 kW at a power factor of 0.8 lagging, on 400 V.

V_L = np.sqrt(3) * V_ph          # 398 V; the nominal 400 V is a rounded value
P = 30e3                          # W
pf0 = 0.8
S0 = P / pf0
Q0 = np.sqrt(S0**2 - P**2)
I0 = S0 / (np.sqrt(3) * V_L)
print(f"S = {S0 / 1e3:.1f} kVA   P = {P / 1e3:.1f} kW   Q = {Q0 / 1e3:.1f} kvar   line current = {I0:.1f} A")

S = 37.5 kVA   P = 30.0 kW   Q = 22.5 kvar   line current = 54.3 A


The motor does 30 kW of work, but the cables carry current for 37.5 kVA. The 22.5 kvar of reactive power is the magnetising current the motor needs to make its field.

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
text:
Power factor correction
Reactive current costs money even though it does no work. It needs bigger cables and transformers, it heats them (\(I^2R\) losses), and many network tariffs charge on kVA demand or penalise a low power factor. A capacitor draws reactive current of the opposite sign, so a capacitor bank across the motor supplies its magnetising current locally. The network then supplies only the real power.
To raise the power factor from \(\cos\phi_1\) to \(\cos\phi_2\), the capacitors must supply:
\[Q_C = P(\tan\phi_1 - \tan\phi_2)\]
The capacitance depends on how the bank is connected. In delta, each capacitor sees the line voltage, so \(C = Q_C / (3\,\omega V_L^2)\). In star, each sees the phase voltage, which is three times smaller squared, so star needs three times the capacitance for the same kvar.

def kvar_needed(P, pf_from, pf_to):
    return P * (np.tan(np.arccos(pf_from)) - np.tan(np.arccos(pf_to)))

pf1 = 0.95
Qc = kvar_needed(P, pf0, pf1)
C_delta = Qc / (3 * w * V_L**2)
C_star = Qc / (3 * w * V_ph**2)
I1 = P / (np.sqrt(3) * V_L * pf1)
pf_check = P / np.hypot(P, Q0 - Qc)

print(f"capacitor bank: {Qc / 1e3:.2f} kvar -> {C_delta * 1e6:.1f} uF per phase in delta, {C_star * 1e6:.1f} uF in star")
print(f"line current {I0:.1f} A -> {I1:.1f} A ({100 * (1 - I1 / I0):.0f} % less); "
      f"cable losses {100 * (1 - (I1 / I0)**2):.0f} % less; new pf {pf_check:.3f}")

targets = np.round(np.arange(0.80, 1.0001, 0.01), 2)
need = [round(kvar_needed(P, pf0, x) / 1e3, 2) for x in targets]
pfc = (
    Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="340px"))
    .add_xaxis([f"{x:.2f}" for x in targets])
    .add_yaxis("capacitor kvar needed", need, symbol_size=6,
               markline_opts=opts.MarkLineOpts(data=[opts.MarkLineItem(x="0.95", name="0.95")],
                                               label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(formatter="target 0.95")))
    .set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=False))
    .set_global_opts(
        title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="Correcting 30 kW from pf 0.80: kvar needed per target"),
        xaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="target pf", boundary_gap=False),
        yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="kvar"),
        tooltip_opts=opts.TooltipOpts(trigger="axis"),
    )
)
pfc.render_notebook()

capacitor bank: 12.64 kvar -> 84.5 uF per phase in delta, 253.5 uF in star
line current 54.3 A -> 45.8 A (16 % less); cable losses 29 % less; new pf 0.950





        




A 12.6 kvar bank cuts the line current by 16 % and the cable losses by 29 %. The chart shows why sites correct to about 0.95 and not to 1.0. The curve steepens near unity, so the last 0.05 of power factor needs almost 10 kvar more capacitance for little extra saving. Over-correcting is a real risk too. With too much capacitance at light load, the site turns leading and can push its local voltage up.

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
section: Why transmission runs at high voltage
text:
Why transmission runs at high voltage
To deliver a power \(P\) at line voltage \(V_L\), the line current is \(I = P / (\sqrt{3}\,V_L \cos\phi)\). The loss in a line with resistance \(R\) per phase is \(3I^2R\). Put the two together:
\[P_{loss} = \frac{P^2 R}{V_L^2 \cos^2\phi}\]
Loss falls with the square of voltage. Double the voltage and the same wires lose a quarter as much. The cell below sends 100 MW down a line of 5 \(\Omega\) per phase, which is roughly 100 km of a typical overhead conductor, at a range of standard Australian voltages.

P_send, R_line, pf_line = 100e6, 5.0, 0.95
kv = [11, 33, 66, 132, 275, 330, 500]
rows = []
for k in kv:
    I_k = P_send / (np.sqrt(3) * k * 1e3 * pf_line)
    loss = 3 * I_k**2 * R_line
    rows.append((k, I_k, loss))
    print(f"{k:4d} kV: line current {I_k:7.0f} A, loss {loss / 1e6:8.2f} MW = {100 * loss / P_send:7.2f} % of the power")

bars = (
    Bar(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="340px"))
    .add_xaxis([f"{k} kV" for k in kv])
    .add_yaxis("loss as % of 100 MW", [round(100 * l / P_send, 3) for _, _, l in rows])
    .set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=True, position="top", formatter="{c} %"))
    .set_global_opts(
        title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="Line loss for 100 MW over 5 ohm per phase (log scale)"),
        yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(type_="log", name="% loss"),
        legend_opts=opts.LegendOpts(is_show=False),
    )
)
bars.render_notebook()

  11 kV: line current    5525 A, loss   457.86 MW =  457.86 % of the power
  33 kV: line current    1842 A, loss    50.87 MW =   50.87 % of the power
  66 kV: line current     921 A, loss    12.72 MW =   12.72 % of the power

At 11 kV the “loss” is several times the power being sent, so the line could not carry it at all. At 330 kV the same wires lose half a percent. This is why the network steps voltage up at the power station, carries bulk power at 220 to 500 kV, steps it down to 132, 66 and 33 kV for sub-transmission, 11 or 22 kV for distribution, and finally 400/230 V at a pole or pad-mount transformer near the customer.
Higher still is not free. Insulators, clearances and towers grow with voltage, and above a few hundred kilovolts the air around a conductor starts to ionise (corona), which itself wastes power. For very long cables, especially under the sea, the capacitance of AC cable becomes the limit, and links such as Basslink between Victoria and Tasmania use high-voltage DC instead.

title: Three-Phase Power Systems
section: How the grid balances supply and demand
text:
How the grid balances supply and demand
A grid stores almost no energy in its wires. Every second, generation must equal demand plus losses. Any mismatch comes out of, or goes into, the kinetic energy of every synchronous generator’s spinning rotor, and that changes the speed of all of them together. Grid frequency is the scoreboard. Too little generation and frequency falls. Too much and it rises. The Australian National Electricity Market (NEM) keeps frequency within 49.85 to 50.15 Hz in normal operation.
Several layers of control respond to a sudden loss of generation, each slower and larger than the one before:








Layer
Acts within
What it does




Inertia
Instantly
Rotors slow down and release stored energy. This only slows the fall; it cannot stop it


Load damping
Instantly
Motor loads draw slightly less power at lower frequency


Primary response (governor droop)
Seconds
Each generator opens up in proportion to the frequency error, which halts the fall at a new, lower frequency


Secondary control
Minutes
Central control nudges generators until frequency is back at 50 Hz (in the NEM, part of the frequency control ancillary services, FCAS)


Dispatch
5 minutes
The NEM re-dispatches generators by price every five minutes: cheapest offers first (the merit order)



The first two layers can be modelled with the swing equation, written per unit (as fractions of system size):
\[2H\,\frac{d\,\Delta f}{dt} = \Delta P_m - \Delta P_{load} - D\,\Delta f\]
\(H\) is the inertia constant: stored kinetic energy divided by rating, in seconds. \(D\) is load damping. A governor with droop \(R\) raises mechanical power by \(\Delta P_m = -\Delta f / R\) in steady state. With 5 % droop, a 5 % fall in frequency drives a generator to full output. Its turbine follows with a lag \(T_g\).
The simulation below trips a 750 MW unit in a 20 GW system. That is 3.75 % of supply, about the size of a large coal unit tripping. It runs once with no governor response and once with half the fleet providing 5 % droop.

H, D = 4.0, 1.0          # s; pu power per pu frequency
dP = 750 / 20000         # pu of system demand: the lost generation
Tg, R_droop = 5.0, 0.05  # governor and turbine lag (s); droop
share = 0.5              # fraction of the fleet with governor headroom

def swing(t, x, k):
    df, dPm = x
    ddf = (dPm - dP - D * df) / (2 * H)
    ddPm = (-(k / R_droop) * df - dPm) / Tg
    return [ddf, ddPm]

t_end = 120
ts = np.linspace(0, t_end, 2401)
runs = {}
for name, k in [("no governor response", 0.0), ("5 % droop on half the fleet", share)]:
    sol = solve_ivp(swing, (0, t_end), [0.0, 0.0], args=(k,), t_eval=ts, rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-10)
    runs[name] = f0 * (1 + sol.y[0])

beta = {"no governor response": D, "5 % droop on half the fleet": D + share / R_droop}
rocof = -dP / (2 * H) * f0
for name, f in runs.items():
    print(f"{name:28s} nadir {f.min():.3f} Hz, settles at {f[-1]:.3f} Hz (predicted {f0 * (1 - dP / beta[name]):.3f} Hz)")
print(f"initial rate of change of frequency: {rocof:.3f} Hz/s")

show = (ts <= 40) & (np.arange(len(ts)) % 4 == 0)   # every 0.2 s keeps the page small
freq = (
    Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="360px"))
    .add_xaxis([f"{x:.1f}" for x in ts[show]])
)
for name, f in runs.items():
    freq.add_yaxis(name, [round(float(x), 4) for x in f[show]], is_symbol_show=False)
freq = freq.set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=False)).set_global_opts(
    title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="Frequency after losing 3.75 % of generation"),
    xaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="s", boundary_gap=False),
    yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="Hz", min_=47.5, max_=50.2),
    tooltip_opts=opts.TooltipOpts(trigger="axis"),
    legend_opts=opts.LegendOpts(pos_top="8%"),
)
freq.render_notebook()

no governor response         nadir 48.125 Hz, settles at 48.125 Hz (predicted 48.125 Hz)
5 % droop on half the fleet  nadir 49.580 Hz, settles at 49.830 Hz (predicted 49.830 Hz)
initial rate of change of frequency: -0.234 Hz/s





        




Inertia sets the opening slope, about 0.23 Hz per second. It is the same in both runs, because no controller has acted yet. Without governors, only load damping resists the fall, and frequency slides towards 48.1 Hz. Long before that, automatic under-frequency load shedding would disconnect blocks of customers to save the system. With droop, the governors catch the fall within seconds. Frequency settles near 49.83 Hz. That is just outside the normal band, which the standard allows while the system recovers from a large trip. It sits below 50 Hz on purpose, because droop needs a frequency error to keep the extra output going. Secondary control then removes that last offset over the following minutes.
The model also shows why the energy transition makes frequency control harder. Solar, wind and batteries connect through inverters and have no spinning mass, so as they displace coal, \(H\) falls and the opening slope steepens. The answer is fast frequency response from batteries, which can inject power within a fraction of a second, plus grid-forming inverters that imitate inertia in software. Since 2017, the Hornsdale battery in South Australia has shown how much faster than a turbine a battery can respond.

title: Network Theorems
text:
Electricity Equations ends at Ohm’s law and Kirchhoff’s laws. Those two laws can solve any linear circuit, but they make you solve the whole circuit every time. The theorems on this page are shortcuts. They let you replace most of a circuit with something much smaller, and then ask questions about the part you care about.
Every theorem here is checked in code against a full nodal solution of the same circuit. If a shortcut and the full solution disagree, the assertions at the end of each section fail.

title: Network Theorems
text:
Linearity is the whole idea
A circuit built from resistors, independent sources and linear dependent sources is linear. Every node voltage and every branch current is a weighted sum of the source values. Double every source and every current doubles. Two consequences follow, and every theorem on this page is one of them.

Superposition. Because the response is a sum, you can find each source’s share separately and add the shares.
Equivalence. Seen from two terminals, a linear network has a straight-line voltage-current characteristic. A straight line needs only two numbers to describe it. So any such network, however large, can be replaced by two elements: a source and a resistance. Thevenin and Norton are the two ways to write that line.

The theorems break as soon as something is not linear. A diode, a saturating transformer core or a transistor at its limits all have curved characteristics. The last section covers what to do then.

title: Network Theorems
text:
The example circuit
One circuit runs through the whole page. It has a voltage source, a current source and three resistors. A load resistor \(R_L\) connects across terminals a and b. The question is always the same: what current flows in \(R_L\), for any value of \(R_L\)?



Example circuit: V1 = 12 V in series with R1 = 4 ohm feeds node A; R3 = 6 ohm runs from A to ground; R2 = 2 ohm joins A to node B; current source Is = 2 A injects into B; load RL sits across terminals a and b. Its Thevenin equivalent is 16 V in series with 4.4 ohm, and its Norton equivalent is 3.64 A in parallel with 4.4 ohm.


The right-hand panels are the answer this page works towards. Seen from terminals a and b, the whole left-hand circuit behaves exactly like a 16 V source behind 4.4 \(\Omega\).

title: Network Theorems
text:
Nodal analysis: the reference answer
Nodal analysis writes Kirchhoff’s current law at every node whose voltage is unknown. Ground is the reference, so the unknowns are \(V_A\) and \(V_B\). Current leaving each node through each branch sums to zero:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}+\frac{1}{R_3} & -\frac{1}{R_2} \\
-\frac{1}{R_2} & \frac{1}{R_2}+\frac{1}{R_L}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} V_A \\ V_B \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} V_1 / R_1 \\ I_s \end{bmatrix}
\]
The matrix is the conductance matrix \(G\). Its diagonal holds the total conductance at each node, and each off-diagonal term is minus the conductance joining two nodes. The right-hand side holds the source currents pushed into each node. Solving \(G\,v = i\) is one call to np.linalg.solve. Circuit simulators such as SPICE build the same matrix, only larger.

import numpy as np
from pyecharts import options as opts
from pyecharts.charts import Line, Bar
from pyecharts.globals import CurrentConfig

# assets.pyecharts.org served an expired TLS cert on 2026-11-11; pin the jsDelivr mirror
CurrentConfig.ONLINE_HOST = "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/pyecharts/pyecharts-assets@f2328d558550046fc5449672a6850e848e141590/assets/v6/"

R1, R2, R3 = 4.0, 2.0, 6.0   # ohm
V1, Is = 12.0, 2.0           # V, A

def solve(V1=V1, Is=Is, RL=np.inf):
    "Node voltages (VA, VB) by nodal analysis. RL=inf leaves terminals a-b open."
    gL = 0.0 if np.isinf(RL) else 1 / RL
    G = np.array([[1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3, -1/R2],
                  [-1/R2,               1/R2 + gL]])
    i = np.array([V1 / R1, Is])
    return np.linalg.solve(G, i)

RL = 10.0
VA, VB = solve(RL=RL)
I_L = VB / RL
print(f"VA = {VA:.4f} V   VB = {VB:.4f} V   I_L = {I_L:.4f} A")

VA = 9.3333 V   VB = 11.1111 V   I_L = 1.1111 A


With a 10 \(\Omega\) load, \(V_B = 11.11\) V and the load carries 1.111 A. Every method below must reproduce that number.

title: Network Theorems
text:
Superposition
Turn off every source except one, solve, and repeat for each source. The real response is the sum of the partial responses.
“Turn off” has a precise meaning. A voltage source switched off is a 0 V source, which is a short circuit. A current source switched off is a 0 A source, which is an open circuit. Getting these backwards is the most common mistake with this theorem.

VB_v1 = solve(V1=V1, Is=0.0, RL=RL)[1]   # Is open
VB_is = solve(V1=0.0, Is=Is, RL=RL)[1]   # V1 shorted
print(f"V1 alone: {VB_v1:.4f} V   Is alone: {VB_is:.4f} V")
print(f"sum:      {VB_v1 + VB_is:.4f} V   full solution: {VB:.4f} V")

P_full = VB**2 / RL
P_parts = VB_v1**2 / RL + VB_is**2 / RL
print(f"load power: full {P_full:.3f} W, sum of partial powers {P_parts:.3f} W")

V1 alone: 5.0000 V   Is alone: 6.1111 V
sum:      11.1111 V   full solution: 11.1111 V
load power: full 12.346 W, sum of partial powers 6.235 W


The voltages add up exactly: 5 V from \(V_1\) plus 6.11 V from \(I_s\) gives 11.11 V. The powers do not. Power goes as voltage squared, and \((a+b)^2 \neq a^2 + b^2\). Superposition works for voltages and currents, never for power. Find the total voltage or current first, then compute power from it.

title: Network Theorems
text:
Source transformation
A voltage source \(V\) in series with a resistor \(R\) and a current source \(V/R\) in parallel with the same \(R\) look identical from their terminals. Both give \(V\) when open-circuited and \(V/R\) when short-circuited. Since a linear two-terminal network is fully described by those two points, the two are interchangeable.
Swapping one form for the other lets you collapse a ladder circuit by hand. Series resistors add in the voltage-source form, and parallel current sources add in the current-source form. The cell below folds the example circuit down to a single source, one step at a time.

def par(a, b):
    return a * b / (a + b)

steps = []
I = V1 / R1                      # 1. V1 + R1 in series  ->  3 A parallel with R1
R = R1
steps.append(("V1, R1 as a current source", I, "A", R))
R = par(R, R3)                   # 2. R3 is now in parallel: combine
steps.append(("absorb R3 in parallel", I, "A", R))
V = I * R; I = None              # 3. back to a voltage source
steps.append(("convert to a voltage source", V, "V", R))
R = R + R2                       # 4. R2 is in series: add
steps.append(("absorb R2 in series", V, "V", R))
I = V / R                        # 5. to a current source, then add Is in parallel
I = I + Is
steps.append(("convert, then add Is in parallel", I, "A", R))

for name, val, unit, r in steps:
    print(f"{name:34s} {val:7.4f} {unit}   with {r:.4f} ohm")

V1, R1 as a current source          3.0000 A   with 4.0000 ohm
absorb R3 in parallel               3.0000 A   with 2.4000 ohm
convert to a voltage source         7.2000 V   with 2.4000 ohm
absorb R2 in series                 7.2000 V   with 4.4000 ohm
convert, then add Is in parallel    3.6364 A   with 4.4000 ohm


Five steps reduce the circuit to a 3.636 A source in parallel with 4.4 \(\Omega\). That is the Norton equivalent in the diagram, found without writing a single equation.

title: Network Theorems
text:
Thevenin equivalent
Thevenin’s theorem: any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a voltage source \(V_{th}\) in series with a resistance \(R_{th}\).

\(V_{th}\) is the open-circuit voltage across the terminals, with no load connected.
\(R_{th}\) is the resistance seen looking into the terminals with every independent source switched off.

There is a second way to find \(R_{th}\): short the terminals, measure the short-circuit current \(I_{sc}\), and take \(R_{th} = V_{oc} / I_{sc}\). This version also works on a real box you cannot open, and on circuits with dependent sources, which cannot be switched off.

V_th = solve(RL=np.inf)[1]                  # open circuit

R_th_off = R2 + par(R1, R3)                 # sources off: V1 shorted, Is open

VA_sc = (V1 / R1) / (1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3)    # terminals shorted: VB = 0
I_sc = VA_sc / R2 + Is
R_th_meas = V_th / I_sc

print(f"V_th = {V_th:.4f} V")
print(f"R_th = {R_th_off:.4f} ohm (sources off)   {R_th_meas:.4f} ohm (Voc / Isc)")
print(f"I_sc = {I_sc:.4f} A")

loads = np.logspace(-1, 3, 200)
I_nodal = np.array([solve(RL=r)[1] / r for r in loads])
I_thev = V_th / (R_th_off + loads)
print(f"worst disagreement over 0.1 to 1000 ohm loads: {np.abs(I_nodal - I_thev).max():.2e} A")

V_th = 16.0000 V
R_th = 4.4000 ohm (sources off)   4.4000 ohm (Voc / Isc)
I_sc = 3.6364 A
worst disagreement over 0.1 to 1000 ohm loads: 8.88e-16 A


Both routes give \(R_{th} = 4.4\ \Omega\). Across 200 load values from 0.1 \(\Omega\) to 1 k\(\Omega\), the two-element model matches the full nodal solution to within rounding error. The left-hand circuit and its Thevenin equivalent cannot be told apart from terminals a and b.

title: Network Theorems
text:
Norton equivalent
Norton’s theorem writes the same straight line the other way: a current source \(I_N = I_{sc}\) in parallel with \(R_N = R_{th}\). Source transformation turns one into the other, so the two theorems are really one result.
Which form to use depends on the load. Thevenin suits a load in series, because the resistances simply add. Norton suits loads in parallel, because conductances add and the current divides. With Norton, the load current is a current divider:
\[I_L = I_N \frac{R_N}{R_N + R_L}\]

I_N, R_N = I_sc, R_th_off
I_norton = I_N * R_N / (R_N + RL)
print(f"I_N = {I_N:.4f} A, R_N = {R_N:.4f} ohm -> I_L = {I_norton:.4f} A (nodal: {I_L:.4f} A)")

I_N = 3.6364 A, R_N = 4.4000 ohm -> I_L = 1.1111 A (nodal: 1.1111 A)

title: Network Theorems
text:
Maximum power transfer
With the circuit reduced to \(V_{th}\) and \(R_{th}\), the power delivered to the load is a one-line function of \(R_L\):
\[P_L = \frac{V_{th}^2 R_L}{(R_{th}+R_L)^2}\]
Setting \(dP_L/dR_L = 0\) gives \(R_L = R_{th}\), and then \(P_{max} = V_{th}^2 / 4R_{th}\). This is the maximum power transfer theorem.
The catch shows up in the efficiency. At the matched point, the same current flows through \(R_{th}\) and \(R_L\), and the two are equal, so exactly half the power is burnt inside the source. The chart shows both curves.

rl = np.round(np.arange(0.2, 40.01, 0.2), 1)
p = V_th**2 * rl / (R_th_off + rl)**2
eff = 100 * rl / (R_th_off + rl)

    Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="380px"))

The power peaks at 14.5 W when \(R_L = 4.4\ \Omega\), at exactly 50 % efficiency. Past the peak, load power falls but efficiency keeps climbing towards 100 %.
That one chart explains why two fields treat this theorem so differently:








Field
Goal
Design choice

Get the most signal out of a weak source
Match the load to the source (\(R_L = R_{th}\); 50 \(\Omega\) RF systems)

title: Network Theorems
text:
When the shortcuts fail

Nonlinear parts. A diode or a solar cell has a curved characteristic, so no single Thevenin pair describes it. Engineers linearise around an operating point instead. The resulting small-signal equivalent is valid only for small changes about that point.
Power. As the superposition section showed, partial powers never add. Superpose voltages or currents, then compute power.
Dependent sources. A source controlled by another voltage or current cannot be switched off. Find \(R_{th}\) from \(V_{oc}/I_{sc}\), or drive the terminals with a test source and measure the ratio.
AC circuits. title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
text:
A single line diagram is the map of an electrical network. It shows what connects to what, at which voltage, through which switches, transformers and protection. Utilities use it to plan, to operate and to keep people safe. A switching operator, a protection engineer and a connection designer all start from the same drawing.
This page builds a typical Australian utility chain, from a 110 kV line down to a 400/230 V customer bus. It explains each part of the drawing. Then it computes the fault level at each bus from the ratings printed on the diagram, and assertions check that the numbers on the drawing match the code.

title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
text:
Why one line is enough
A power network carries three phases, so a full wiring diagram needs three conductors for every connection. An SLD draws one. That works because a utility network is designed to be balanced. The three phases carry equal currents, 120 degrees apart, so one phase tells you everything about the other two. Three-Phase Power Systems covers this per-phase idea in depth.
So one line on an SLD stands for all three phases of a circuit (and the neutral, where there is one). A breaker drawn once is a three-pole breaker. A transformer drawn as two circles is a three-phase transformer.
The single line view stops being enough in three cases:

Unbalanced faults. A single phase to earth fault breaks the symmetry. Protection studies then use symmetrical components, and the SLD only supplies the data.
Secondary wiring. CT and VT connections, relay inputs and trip circuits need a three line diagram or a schematic, which shows each phase.
Single phase parts of the network. Rural single wire earth return (SWER) lines and single phase LV services are drawn on the same SLD, but the line no longer means three phases. The drawing labels them.

text:

Breaker state matters as much as the symbol. Many utilities draw a closed breaker filled and an open one hollow, and mark a deliberately open device N/O (normally open). On a live operating diagram the state is updated as switching happens.
North American drawings follow ANSI/IEEE conventions instead of IEC. The topology reads the same way. The breaker symbol differs, and protection is shown as numbered device circles. The numbers are listed below.

title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
text:
Reading a utility SLD



Example utility SLD. Two 110 kV lines feed a zone substation through disconnectors and breakers with distance protection into two 110/11 kV 25 MVA transformers with 10 percent impedance. Each transformer feeds an 11 kV bus; a normally open bus section breaker joins bus A and bus B. Four 11 kV feeders leave through breakers with 50/51 overcurrent protection. Feeder F2 runs several km to a distribution substation: an HV fuse, an 11 kV / 433 V 500 kVA 4 percent Dyn11 transformer, an LV main breaker and a 400/230 V bus with three fused LV circuits. A normally open point between F2 and F3 allows backfeed. Fault levels are 11.7 kA at 11 kV with the bus section open, 21.0 kA with it closed, and 15.8 kA at the LV bus.


Read an SLD in the direction power flows, from source to load. On this drawing that is top to bottom:

Sources. Two 110 kV lines come in from the transmission or sub-transmission network. Each passes a disconnector, a breaker and a CT. The breaker carries distance protection (21), which measures impedance to decide whether a fault is on its own line.
Transformation. Each line feeds its own 110/11 kV zone transformer. The label gives the ratio, the rating (25 MVA) and the impedance (10%). Differential protection (87T) compares current in and out and trips both sides for an internal fault.
Busbars. Each transformer feeds one section of the 11 kV bus. The bus section breaker between them is normally open, so each transformer carries its own half of the load. The next section shows why the open tie matters.
Feeders. Four 11 kV feeders leave the bus, each through a breaker with overcurrent and earth fault protection (50/51). A feeder runs for kilometres as overhead line or cable.
Distribution substation. Along feeder F2, a fuse protects a 500 kVA, 11 kV / 433 V transformer. Its secondary is set about 8% above 400 V, so that voltage at the end of the LV circuits stays within limits under load. An LV main breaker feeds the 400/230 V bus. Fused LV circuits leave the bus for customers.
Alternate supply. A normally open point joins the end of F2 to F3. If F2’s breaker trips for a fault near the zone substation, operators isolate the faulted section and close this point. F3 then supplies the rest of F2 from the other side.

The colours follow voltage level, a common habit on utility drawings, so a glance shows where each transformer changes voltage.

title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
section: Switching state and normally open points
text:
Switching state and normally open points
An SLD shows two different things. The design is what is built. The state is which devices are open or closed right now. Utility control rooms keep an operating diagram with live state, and every switching program is written against it.
Normally open points are the key to reading a distribution network. Most urban 11 kV networks are built as meshes or rings, but they are run radially: one source per section, with an open point somewhere in each loop. A radial run keeps protection simple, because fault current flows only one way. It also keeps fault levels down. When a section fails, operators move the open point to restore supply from another feeder.
For safe work, the SLD is where isolation is planned. The usual sequence is:

Open the breaker to interrupt current.
Open the disconnectors on both sides to make a visible break.
Lock and tag the open devices.
Test that the section is dead.
Close earth switches, or apply portable earths, on both sides.

A missing backfeed path on the drawing is how people get hurt. Embedded generation such as rooftop solar and batteries adds paths that older drawings never showed.

title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
section: Worked example: fault level down the SLD
text:
Worked example: fault level down the SLD
The ratings on the diagram are enough to compute the three-phase fault current at every bus. The method is per-unit. Each impedance is expressed as a fraction of a common base power, \(S_{base}\), so impedances on both sides of a transformer can be added directly without referring them through the turns ratio.
Three steps do the work. Convert each element to per-unit on the common base:
\[ Z_{pu} = \frac{Z\%}{100} \cdot \frac{S_{base}}{S_{rated}} \]
Add the per-unit impedances in series from the source to the faulted bus. Then convert the total back to fault power and current:
\[ S_{fault} = \frac{S_{base}}{Z_{total}} \qquad I_{fault} = \frac{S_{fault}}{\sqrt{3}\, V_{LL}} \]
The upstream grid is given by its fault level at 110 kV, here 2000 MVA, which converts to an impedance the same way. Resistance, feeder impedance and motor contribution are ignored. That gives slightly high, so conservative, currents, which is the safe direction for sizing switchgear.


import math

S_BASE_MVA = 100.0

def source_z(fault_mva, s_base=S_BASE_MVA):
    "Per-unit impedance of the upstream grid, from its fault level."
    return s_base / fault_mva

def transformer_z(z_pct, rating_mva, s_base=S_BASE_MVA):
    "Transformer impedance moved from its own rating onto the common base."
    return z_pct / 100 * s_base / rating_mva

def fault_level(z_pu, kv, s_base=S_BASE_MVA):
    "Three-phase fault MVA and kA at a bus whose total source impedance is z_pu."
    mva = s_base / z_pu
    return mva, mva / (math.sqrt(3) * kv)


from IPython.display import Markdown

z_grid = source_z(2000)       # 110 kV grid fault level
z_zone = transformer_z(10, 25)  # each 110/11 kV zone transformer
z_dist = transformer_z(4, 0.5)  # 11 kV / 433 V distribution transformer

buses = {
    "110 kV bus": (z_grid, 110),
    "11 kV bus, section N/O": (z_grid + z_zone, 11),
    "11 kV bus, section closed": (z_grid + z_zone / 2, 11),
    "400 V bus": (z_grid + z_zone + z_dist, 0.433),
    "400 V bus, infinite grid": (z_dist, 0.433),
}

results = {name: (z, *fault_level(z, kv)) for name, (z, kv) in buses.items()}

Three things come out of the table.

Closing the bus section nearly doubles the 11 kV fault level, from 11.7 kA to 21.0 kA, because the two transformers then feed a fault in parallel. That is why the tie runs normally open. Closing it would also push all switchgear on both buses closer to its 25 kA breaking rating. The tie is closed only briefly, during load transfers, after checking the result against the rating.
The LV fault level depends almost entirely on the distribution transformer. Its 8 pu dwarfs the 0.45 pu upstream. Even an infinitely strong grid would only raise the 400 V fault current from 15.8 kA to 16.7 kA. So LV switchboard ratings can be set from the transformer nameplate alone, which is why connection rules quote prospective fault current by transformer size.
The same walk works on any SLD. An SLD is a graph whose edges carry impedances. A fault study adds the impedances along the path from each source to the faulted bus, and combines parallel paths. Commercial tools such as PowerFactory or ETAP do exactly this on networks with thousands of buses, and handle the unbalanced cases with symmetrical components.
