title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
text:
Australian practice

Voltages. Transmission runs at 275 or 330 kV, and up to 500 kV in the southern states. Sub-transmission runs at 132, 110, 66 or 33 kV. Distribution is mostly 11 kV, with 22 kV in some states and SWER lines in rural areas. Low voltage is 400/230 V under AS 60038.
Symbols. Drawings use IEC 60617 style symbols. Older drawings may use the earlier AS 1102 series.
Who owns which SLD. Each distribution network service provider (DNSP), such as Energex or Ergon Energy in Queensland, keeps its own drafting standards and the operating diagram for its network. Customer installations behind the connection point are the customer’s drawing.
When you will be asked for one. HV customer connections and embedded generation connections (solar, batteries, generators) normally need an SLD with the connection application. The DNSP checks protection, export limits and fault level contribution against it. Inverter systems are installed to AS/NZS 4777.1, and a clear SLD is part of the standard handover documentation.

title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
text:
Checklist for reading any SLD

Find the sources: grid supply, generators and inverters.
Follow power from each source to the loads.
Note each voltage level and where transformers change it.
Note every open device, and every normally open point.
Identify the bus arrangement, and what one fault takes out.
Read the protection numbers on each breaker.
Check the fault level at each bus against the switchgear rating.
Look for backfeed paths, especially from embedded generation.

title: Utility Single Line Diagrams
text:
Not covered here

Protection grading. How time-current curves on 50/51 relays and fuses are coordinated so that the device nearest the fault trips first.
Unbalanced faults. Symmetrical components, and single phase to earth fault currents, which depend on transformer vector group and earthing.
X/R ratio and peak current. The asymmetric first-cycle current that switchgear must withstand, which the simple calculation above ignores.
Earthing systems. MEN (multiple earthed neutral) in Australian LV installations, and step and touch voltage at substations.
Arc flash. Incident energy studies, which start from the bus fault levels computed here.

title: Filter Design
text:
A filter keeps the frequencies you want and rejects the rest. This page designs filters for one concrete job: a sensor produces a slow 5 Hz signal, sampled at 1 kHz, and mains wiring couples 50 Hz hum and broadband noise into it. The design target is at least 40 dB of rejection at 50 Hz, with less than 0.5 dB of loss at 5 Hz.
The page starts with a single resistor and capacitor, shows why that is not enough, then moves through filter order and the standard families, sampling and aliasing, and finally digital FIR and IIR filters applied to a real signal. It complements FFT Examples, which uses Fourier terms to forecast but never designs a filter.

title: Filter Design
section: RC filters: the first-order building block
text:
RC filters: the first-order building block



RC low-pass: a series resistor R from Vin to the output node and a capacitor C from that node to ground, so it passes frequencies below fc = 1/(2 pi R C). RC high-pass: the same two parts swapped, with a series capacitor and a resistor to ground, so it passes frequencies above fc.


A capacitor’s impedance \(1/(j\omega C)\) falls as frequency rises. In the low-pass circuit, it forms a voltage divider with \(R\) that shorts high frequencies to ground:
\[H(j\omega) = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{1}{1 + j\omega RC} \qquad f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}\]
At the cutoff frequency \(f_c\), the output is \(1/\sqrt{2}\) of the input, which is \(-3\) dB, and the phase lags 45 degrees. Above \(f_c\), the gain falls at 20 dB per decade, a factor of 10 for every factor of 10 in frequency. The high-pass version swaps the parts and mirrors the response.

Try a 10 k\(\Omega\) resistor and a 1 \(\mu\)F capacitor, which put \(f_c\) at 15.9 Hz, between the signal and the hum:

import numpy as np
from pyecharts import options as opts
from pyecharts.charts import Line, Bar
from pyecharts.globals import CurrentConfig

# assets.pyecharts.org served an expired TLS cert on 2026-11-11; pin the jsDelivr mirror
CurrentConfig.ONLINE_HOST = "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/pyecharts/pyecharts-assets@f2328d558550046fc5449672a6850e848e141590/assets/v6/"
from scipy import signal

fs = 1000.0                       # Hz, sample rate
f_sig, f_hum = 5.0, 50.0          # Hz
R, C = 10e3, 1e-6
fc_rc = 1 / (2 * np.pi * R * C)

def db(h):
    return 20 * np.log10(np.abs(h))

def rc_lowpass(f):
    return 1 / (1 + 1j * 2 * np.pi * f * R * C)

print(f"fc = {fc_rc:.1f} Hz")
print(f"at  5 Hz: {db(rc_lowpass(f_sig)):6.2f} dB   (target: better than -0.5 dB)")
print(f"at 50 Hz: {db(rc_lowpass(f_hum)):6.2f} dB   (target: -40 dB or lower)")

fc = 15.9 Hz
at  5 Hz:  -0.41 dB   (target: better than -0.5 dB)
at 50 Hz: -10.36 dB   (target: -40 dB or lower)


The RC filter fails both targets at once. It removes only 10 dB of hum, and it already costs 0.4 dB of the signal, which is close to the limit. Moving \(f_c\) down helps the hum and hurts the signal. A first-order slope of 20 dB per decade is too gentle when the frequencies to keep and to reject are only a factor of 10 apart. The fix is a steeper slope, which means a higher order.

text:
Order and filter families
An \(N\)th-order filter has \(N\) energy-storing elements (capacitors or inductors), or the digital equivalent. Its slope beyond cutoff is \(20N\) dB per decade. For a fixed order, there is still a choice of shape, and each classic family optimises one property:

Optimises

title: Filter Design
text:
Sampling and aliasing
A digital filter only ever sees samples. Sampling at \(f_s\) can represent frequencies up to the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\), here 500 Hz. Anything above it does not disappear. It aliases: it folds back and appears as a lower frequency that the samples cannot tell apart from a real one.
The cell shows a 950 Hz tone sampled at 1 kHz. Its samples are exactly those of a 50 Hz tone, inverted. Once it is sampled, no digital filter can separate it from real mains hum.

n = np.arange(40)
tn = n / fs
s950 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 950 * tn)
s50 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * tn)
print("950 Hz samples:", np.round(s950[:6], 3))
print(" 50 Hz samples:", np.round(s50[:6], 3))
print(f"largest |s950 + s50| over 40 samples: {np.abs(s950 + s50).max():.1e}")

950 Hz samples: [ 0.    -0.309 -0.588 -0.809 -0.951 -1.   ]
 50 Hz samples: [0.    0.309 0.588 0.809 0.951 1.   ]
largest |s950 + s50| over 40 samples: 1.9e-14


This is why every analog-to-digital converter needs an anti-aliasing filter: an analog low-pass ahead of the converter that removes everything above \(f_s/2\) while it is still separable. Digital filtering can only clean up what survives sampling.

title: Filter Design
text:
Digital filters: FIR and IIR
There are two kinds of digital filter.
A FIR (finite impulse response) filter computes each output as a weighted sum of recent inputs: \(y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k\,x[n-k]\). It has no feedback, so it is always stable. With symmetric weights, it has linear phase: every frequency is delayed by the same \(M/2\) samples, so wave shapes are preserved. The cost is length: sharp responses need many taps. The window method (firwin) truncates the ideal impulse response and tapers it with a window, here Hamming, to control ripple.
An IIR (infinite impulse response) filter also feeds back past outputs: \(y[n] = \sum b_k x[n-k] - \sum a_k y[n-k]\). It reaches a given sharpness with far fewer coefficients, because it is the digital twin of an analog filter. butter(..., fs=...) maps an analog Butterworth into discrete time with the bilinear transform. Its phase is not linear, and high-order IIR filters are numerically fragile, so they are run as a cascade of second-order sections (SOS).
A third option targets one frequency: a notch filter removes a narrow band around 50 Hz and leaves everything else, noise included.

numtaps = 101
fir = signal.firwin(numtaps, fc, window="hamming", fs=fs)
iir = signal.butter(6, fc, output="sos", fs=fs)
b_n, a_n = signal.iirnotch(f_hum, Q=30, fs=fs)

fd = np.linspace(0.5, 150, 300)
h = {
    "FIR, 101 taps": signal.freqz(fir, worN=fd, fs=fs)[1],
    "IIR Butterworth N=6": signal.sosfreqz(iir, worN=fd, fs=fs)[1],
    "IIR notch at 50 Hz": signal.freqz(b_n, a_n, worN=fd, fs=fs)[1],
}

    print(f"{name:20s} at 5 Hz {np.interp(5, fd, g):6.2f} dB   at 50 Hz {np.interp(50, fd, g):7.1f} dB   "
          f"multiplies per sample {cost[name]}")

for name, hh in h.items():

Both low-pass designs meet the target. The FIR needs 101 multiplies per sample. The 6th-order IIR needs 15, in three second-order sections. On a small microcontroller, that difference decides the design. The notch removes the hum with only 5 multiplies, but it passes everything else, so the broadband noise stays.

title: Filter Design
section: Filtering a signal, and the cost of delay
text:
Filtering a signal, and the cost of delay
Now the filters meet a signal. Two seconds of a 5 Hz sine, plus 50 Hz hum at 0.8 of its size, plus white noise, all sampled at 1 kHz. Each filter is scored by the RMS (root mean square) error against the clean sine, ignoring 0.2 s at each end where the filters start up.
A causal filter, one that only uses past samples, must delay its output. For the IIR filter, the delay varies with frequency. The cell measures it at 5 Hz by cross-correlation. Zero-phase filtering (sosfiltfilt) runs the filter forwards and then backwards, so the two phase shifts cancel. It needs the whole recording, so it only works offline.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = np.arange(0, 2.0, 1 / fs)
clean = np.sin(2 * np.pi * f_sig * t)
noisy = clean + 0.8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f_hum * t) + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(t.size)

out = {
    "noisy input": noisy,
    "FIR (delay removed)": np.roll(signal.lfilter(fir, 1.0, noisy), -(numtaps - 1) // 2),
    "IIR causal": signal.sosfilt(iir, noisy),
    "IIR zero-phase": signal.sosfiltfilt(iir, noisy),
}
core = (t > 0.2) & (t < 1.8)

def rms_err(y):
    return np.sqrt(np.mean((y[core] - clean[core]) ** 2))

lags = np.arange(0, 100)
xc = [np.dot(out["IIR causal"][core], np.roll(clean, k)[core]) for k in lags]
delay = lags[int(np.argmax(xc))]
aligned = np.roll(out["IIR causal"], -delay)

for name, y in out.items():
    print(f"{name:22s} RMS error {rms_err(y):.3f}")
print(f"IIR causal delay at 5 Hz: {delay} samples = {delay / fs * 1e3:.0f} ms; "
      f"after removing it the RMS error is {rms_err(aligned):.3f}")

idx = np.where((t >= 0.6) & (t < 1.0))[0][::2]
sig = Line(init_opts=opts.InitOpts(width="100%", height="360px")).add_xaxis([f"{x:.3f}" for x in t[idx]])
sig.add_yaxis("noisy input", [round(float(v), 3) for v in noisy[idx]], is_symbol_show=False,
              linestyle_opts=opts.LineStyleOpts(width=1, opacity=0.5))
sig.add_yaxis("clean 5 Hz", [round(float(v), 3) for v in clean[idx]], is_symbol_show=False,
              linestyle_opts=opts.LineStyleOpts(type_="dashed"))
sig.add_yaxis("IIR causal", [round(float(v), 3) for v in out["IIR causal"][idx]], is_symbol_show=False)
sig.add_yaxis("IIR zero-phase", [round(float(v), 3) for v in out["IIR zero-phase"][idx]], is_symbol_show=False)
sig = sig.set_series_opts(label_opts=opts.LabelOpts(is_show=False)).set_global_opts(
    title_opts=opts.TitleOpts(title="0.4 s of the signal before and after filtering"),
    xaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="s", boundary_gap=False),
    yaxis_opts=opts.AxisOpts(name="value"),
    tooltip_opts=opts.TooltipOpts(trigger="axis"),
    legend_opts=opts.LegendOpts(pos_top="8%"),
)
sig.render_notebook()

FIR (delay removed)    RMS error 0.056
IIR causal             RMS error 0.661
IIR zero-phase         RMS error 0.059
IIR causal delay at 5 Hz: 31 samples = 31 ms; after removing it the RMS error is 0.061





        




The zero-phase IIR and the delay-corrected FIR both recover the 5 Hz sine almost exactly. The residual error is the small slice of noise that falls inside the 20 Hz passband, and no low-pass filter can remove that. The causal IIR output is just as clean, but it arrives late. Scored against the clean signal at the same instant, the 31 ms lag makes it score worse than the unfiltered input. With its delay removed, its error matches the others.
The delay is the real price of causal filtering, and sharper filters pay more of it. In a control loop like the one in Control Systems, that delay is phase lag, and it eats directly into the phase margin. That is why loop sensors are filtered as lightly as possible, and why heavy filtering belongs in logging and analysis, where zero-phase filtering is free.

title: Nixtla - Electricity Load Forecast
text:
Some time series are generated from very low frequency data. These data generally exhibit multiple seasonalities. For example, hourly data may exhibit repeated patterns every hour (every 24 observations) or every day (every 24 * 7, hours per day, observations). This is the case for electricity load. Electricity load may vary hourly, e.g., during the evenings electricity consumption may be expected to increase. But also, the electricity load varies by week. Perhaps on weekends there is an increase in electrical activity.
In this example we will show how to model the two seasonalities of the time series to generate accurate forecasts in a short time. We will use hourly PJM electricity load data. The original data can be found here.

We clearly observe that the time series exhibits seasonal patterns. Moreover, the time series contains 32,896 observations, so it is necessary to use very computationally efficient methods to display them in production.


MSTL model
The MSTL (Multiple Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS) model, originally developed by Kasun Bandara, Rob J Hyndman and Christoph Bergmeir, decomposes the time series in multiple seasonalities using a Local Polynomial Regression (LOESS). Then it forecasts the trend using a custom non-seasonal model and each seasonality using a SeasonalNaive model.
StatsForecast contains a fast implementation of the MSTL model. Also, the decomposition of the time series can be calculated.
First we must define the model parameters. As mentioned before, the electricity load presents seasonalities every 24 hours (Hourly) and every 24 * 7 (Daily) hours. Therefore, we will use [24, 24 * 7] as the seasonalities that the MSTL model receives. We must also specify the manner in which the trend will be forecasted. In this case we will use the AutoARIMA model.

intervals = ConformalIntervals()

mstl = MSTL(
    season_length=[24, 24 * 7], # seasonalities of the time series 
    trend_forecaster=AutoARIMA(), # model used to forecast trend
    prediction_intervals = intervals
)

Once the model is instantiated, we have to instantiate the StatsForecast class to create forecasts.

sf = StatsForecast(
    models=[mstl], # model used to fit each time series 
    freq='H', # frequency of the data
    fallback_model = SeasonalNaive(season_length=7)
)

sf = sf.fit(df=df)

section: 3. How a Hobby Servo Is Controlled: PWM
text:
3. How a Hobby Servo Is Controlled: PWM
Hobby servos are commanded by a 50 Hz PWM signal (one pulse every 20 ms). The pulse width, not the duty cycle percentage, sets the angle:



Pulse width
Position (typical)




1.0 ms
0 degrees (full left)


1.5 ms
90 degrees (center)


2.0 ms
180 degrees (full right)



|<-------------- 20 ms period (50 Hz) -------------->|
 __                                                  __
|  |________________________________________________|  |____ ...
|<>|  1.0-2.0 ms high pulse encodes the target angle
The servo’s internal controller drives the motor until the potentiometer reading matches the commanded pulse, then holds. Note: exact endpoints vary by servo (some are 500-2500 us); calibrate per unit.

title: Servo Motors
Servo Motors
text:
5. Industrial Servos and Closed-Loop Control
Industrial servos pair a BLDC/PMSM motor with a high-resolution encoder (or resolver) and a servo drive that closes the loop in real time. Control is typically nested (cascaded) loops:
Position cmd -> [Position loop] -> [Velocity loop] -> [Current/Torque loop] -> Motor
                     ^                   ^                    ^
                  encoder            encoder             current sensor

Current (torque) loop runs fastest (kHz), regulating motor current via Field-Oriented Control (FOC).
Velocity loop sits on top, regulating speed.
Position loop is outermost, commanding the target angle/position.
Each loop is usually a PID controller; tuning gains (P, I, D) trades off responsiveness vs. overshoot vs. stability.

Command interfaces: step/direction pulses, analog +-10V, or fieldbus (EtherCAT, CANopen, Modbus). Motion is programmed as position/velocity/torque targets or full trajectories (trapezoidal or S-curve profiles).

title: Servo Motors
text:
6. Tuning and Motion Profiles

PID tuning: Raise P for stiffness until it starts to oscillate, add D to damp overshoot, add I to remove steady-state error. Too much I causes wind-up and hunting.
Trapezoidal profile: Accelerate, cruise at constant velocity, decelerate. Simple and common.
S-curve profile: Smooths the acceleration itself (limits jerk) for gentler, quieter motion and less mechanical wear.
Feedforward: Adds a predicted torque/velocity term so the loop does not have to react to everything, improving tracking.

title: Brushless Motors (BLDC / PMSM)
text:
In a brushed motor, brushes physically switch current in the spinning rotor. In a brushless motor that switching is done electronically, outside the motor:

Rotor: permanent magnets (no windings, no brushes).
Stator: three phase windings (A, B, C).
Controller (ESC): energizes the phases in the right sequence based on rotor position.




Benefit
Why




High efficiency
No brush friction/resistance (85-95%).


Long life
Nothing wears but the bearings.


High power density
Windings on stator shed heat easily.


Quiet, low EMI
No brush sparking.



BLDC vs PMSM: physically similar. BLDC is optimized for trapezoidal back-EMF and six-step drive; PMSM has sinusoidal back-EMF and is driven with FOC for smooth torque. In practice the same hardware is often driven either way.
Inrunner vs outrunner: inrunner spins an internal rotor (high RPM, e.g. drills); outrunner spins the outer bell (high torque at lower RPM, e.g. drones, gimbals).

title: Brushless Motors (BLDC / PMSM)
text:
2. Commutation: Making It Spin
The controller must energize the three phases in a rotating pattern synced to the rotor. It uses a 3-phase inverter: six MOSFETs (three half-bridges), one pair per phase.
        +V
         |
   [Q1] [Q3] [Q5]   <- high-side switches
    |    |    |
    A----B----C  ---> motor phases
    |    |    |
   [Q2] [Q4] [Q6]   <- low-side switches
         |
        GND

2.1. Six-Step (Trapezoidal)
There are 6 commutation states per electrical revolution. At any moment one phase is +, one is -, one floats. The controller advances through the 6 states as the rotor turns.


2.2. FOC (Field-Oriented Control / Sinusoidal)
Instead of 6 discrete states, FOC continuously computes the ideal current vector to keep the stator field 90 degrees ahead of the rotor field for maximum torque. It transforms the 3 phase currents into a rotating (d-q) frame, runs PI loops on torque (q) and flux (d), and modulates the inverter with SVPWM. Result: smooth torque, no torque ripple, high efficiency down to zero speed.

title: Brushless Motors (BLDC / PMSM)
text:
3. Rotor Position Sensing
The controller must know where the rotor is to commutate correctly.








Method
How
Trade-off




Hall sensors
3 Hall-effect sensors report the 6 sectors.
Reliable from zero speed; extra wires.


Sensorless (back-EMF)
Measure voltage on the floating phase.
No sensors; poor at very low/zero speed.


Encoder / resolver
High-resolution absolute/incremental position.
Needed for FOC servos; costlier.



Sensorless six-step is why drone motors need an initial spin-up ramp: below a few hundred RPM the back-EMF is too small to read.

title: Brushless Motors (BLDC / PMSM)
section: 4. The ESC and How It Is Controlled
text:
4. The ESC and How It Is Controlled
An Electronic Speed Controller (ESC) contains the 3-phase inverter + the commutation logic. You do not switch phases yourself; you send the ESC a throttle/speed command.







ESC type
Command interface




Hobby / RC ESC
50 Hz PWM, 1.0-2.0 ms pulse = throttle (like a servo).


DShot (digital)
Packetized digital throttle; noise-immune, telemetry.


Industrial drive
Torque/velocity/position over analog or fieldbus.



So at the top level a hobby BLDC is commanded exactly like a servo: a 1.0-2.0 ms pulse at 50 Hz where 1.0 ms = stop and 2.0 ms = full throttle. The ESC translates that into commutation internally.

title: Brushless Motors (BLDC / PMSM)
Brushless Motors (BLDC / PMSM)
text:
6. Practical Considerations

Kv rating: RPM per volt (no load). High Kv = fast/low torque (racing props); low Kv = slow/high torque (heavy lift, gimbals).
Arming and calibration: Hobby ESCs need a throttle-range calibration and an arming sequence; skipping it causes no-spin or runaway.
Pole pairs: Electrical revolutions = pole pairs x mechanical revolutions; FOC needs the correct count.
Timing/advance: Six-step ESCs advance commutation timing with speed for efficiency.
Cooling and current: High power density means real heat; match ESC current rating to the motor and add airflow.
Safety: Props/loads can spin up instantly; bench-test with the load secured.
